items.q: Since my brother (A) moves to Da Nang last year, he (B) has been working at a small hotel (C) near the beach, (D) which belongs to his uncle.
items.explanation: A finished action with a past time marker (last year) takes the past simple; the present simple moves is wrong after since + past event.

items.q: The number of students who (A) take part in the science club (B) have doubled since the school (C) bought new equipment (D) for the laboratory.
items.explanation: The number of + plural noun is a singular subject, so the verb must be singular: has doubled.

items.q: My grandparents, (A) who live in the countryside, always send (B) us fresh vegetables, and my mother cooks (C) it for dinner (D) on Sundays.
items.explanation: The pronoun refers back to fresh vegetables, a plural noun, so it must be the plural object pronoun them.

items.q: The teacher explained the experiment (A) so clearly that even the weakest students (B) were able to understand (C) why the water boiled (D) in a lower temperature on the mountain.
items.explanation: We say something happens at a temperature, not in a temperature, just as with at a high speed or at that level.

items.q: Running in the morning is (A) more healthier than running at night because the air (B) is cleaner and the body (C) has more energy (D) after a good sleep.
items.explanation: A two-syllable adjective ending in -y forms its comparative with -ier; adding more as well creates a double comparative.

items.q: The (A) discovery of penicillin in 1928 was (B) extreme important because it gave doctors (C) a way to treat infections that (D) had killed millions of people.
items.explanation: An adjective (important) is modified by an adverb, so the word must be extremely, not the adjective extreme.

items.q: My grandfather, (A) who had been ill for months, (B) was finally allowed to go home, and the nurse (C) which had looked after him (D) came to say goodbye.
items.explanation: The relative pronoun which is used for things; a person (the nurse) needs who or that.

items.q: (A) Even if we leave right now, we (B) won't arrive at the station on time (C) unless the traffic (D) will be lighter than usual.
items.explanation: In a first conditional the clause after unless (like if) takes the present simple, not will: unless the traffic is lighter.

items.q: (A) When I complained about my missing headphones, my sister asked me (B) where did I leave them and suggested (C) that I (D) should look under the sofa.
items.explanation: A reported question keeps statement word order and shifts the tense back: asked me where I had left them, with no auxiliary did.

items.q: Nam (A) did a mistake in the last question of the maths test, (B) which cost him (C) two marks and the first prize (D) he had hoped for.
items.explanation: The verb that collocates with mistake is make, not do: make a mistake.

items.q: The match was postponed (A) because of the heavy rain, (B) and the fans, (C) despite they were disappointed, (D) waited patiently for the announcement.
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and is followed by a noun or -ing form; a clause with a subject and verb needs the conjunction although or even though.

items.q: When (A) our class grew to forty students, the teachers (B) had to move us (C) because the old room wasn't (D) enough big for everyone.
items.explanation: Enough comes after an adjective (big enough) but before a noun (enough space).

items.q: Our teacher gave us (A) a lot of homework last week, but (B) little of the exercises were (C) really difficult, so I finished them (D) in one evening.
items.explanation: Little is used with uncountable nouns; exercises is a plural countable noun, so the quantifier must be few.

items.q: The doctor advised my father (A) to give up smoking, (B) but he (C) is used to smoke a packet a day and (D) finds it hard to stop.
items.explanation: Be used to means 'be accustomed to' and is followed by a noun or -ing form; only used to (past habit) takes the bare infinitive.

items.q: The news about the earthquake (A) were so shocking that (B) many people (C) stayed up all night (D) watching the reports on television.
items.explanation: News looks plural but is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb: the news was.

items.q: By the time the rescue team (A) arrived at the cave, the boys (B) had been inside for nine days, and their families (C) are waiting anxiously (D) at the entrance.
items.explanation: The whole sentence describes a past situation, so the action in progress at that past moment needs the past continuous, not the present continuous.

items.q: (A) On the end of the term, every student (B) has to give a short presentation (C) about a topic (D) they have chosen themselves.
options: On the end of the term
items.correction: At the end of the term
items.explanation: The fixed expression is at the end of a period of time; on is used with days and dates, not with the end.

items.q: Last week the headmaster announced that the school (A) would organise a trip to Hue (B) in April and that every student (C) who wanted to go (D) must register by tomorrow.
items.correction: had to register by the following day
items.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb, time expressions shift: tomorrow becomes the next/following day, and must is usually reported as had to.

items.q: The Amazon River, (A) which flows through several countries, (B) carries more water (C) than any other river (D) in world.
items.explanation: World is a unique thing and always takes the definite article in this phrase: in the world.

items.q: Mount Fansipan is (A) the highest mountain in Vietnam, but it is (B) not as high (C) than Mount Everest, (D) which is nearly three times as high.
options: which is nearly three times as high
items.explanation: The comparison of equality is (not) as + adjective + as; than belongs only with a comparative form such as higher than.

items.q: My parents (A) don't let me (B) to stay up late on school nights (C) because they believe (D) that sleep is important for learning.
items.explanation: Let + object is followed by the bare infinitive (let me stay), unlike allow, which takes to + verb.

items.q: The village (A) which we grew up has changed a lot, and most of the old wooden houses (B) have been replaced by (C) modern buildings (D) made of concrete.
items.explanation: Which would have to be the object of the verb, but grew up takes no object; a place where something happens needs the relative adverb where (or in which).

items.q: (A) Although he was exhausted after the marathon, the winner (B) stayed on the stage to (C) tell a short speech and (D) thank his coach.
items.explanation: The verb that collocates with speech is give or make; we do not tell a speech.

items.q: (A) After studying in Australia for three years, my aunt (B) speaks fluently English and now (C) works as an interpreter (D) for a large shipping company.
items.explanation: An adverb of manner does not come between a verb and its object; the order is verb + object + adverb: speaks English fluently.

items.q: Unless you (A) don't water these plants every day, they (B) will dry up quickly (C) because the weather (D) has been extremely hot this month.
items.explanation: Unless already means if ... not, so the verb after it must be positive; a negative verb creates a double negative.

items.q: Each of the players (A) on the school team (B) has to attend training three times a week, and (C) the coach (D) don't accept any excuses.
items.explanation: The coach is a third-person singular subject, so the present simple negative is doesn't accept.

items.q: My best friend (A) is good at maths, but she (B) is not very keen (C) with history, (D) which she finds boring.
items.explanation: The adjective keen takes the preposition on when it means 'interested in': keen on history.

items.q: I (A) am looking forward to (B) see my old classmates at the reunion (C) next month, (D) which will be held at our former school.
items.explanation: In look forward to, the word to is a preposition, so it is followed by the -ing form: looking forward to seeing.

items.q: Tomorrow we can either take the bus (A) to the museum (B) or walk there, (C) but we must leave early (D) so as we see everything before it closes.
items.correction: so that we can see everything
items.explanation: A purpose clause with a subject and verb is introduced by so that; so as is only used with to + infinitive (so as to see).

items.q: The more you practise (A) speaking English, (B) the more confident you become, and (C) the exam will seem (D) much more easier.
items.explanation: Easy forms its comparative with -ier, so more easier is a double comparative; the correct form is much easier.
